t: Maximum Profitable Triplets With Increasing Prices I — Left/Right Best Profit
o: For each middle item j we need the best profit among earlier items with strictly smaller price (left[j]) and among later items with strictly larger price (right[j]); the answer is the max of left[j]+profits[j]+right[j]. With n ≤ 2000, an O(n^2) double scan per middle element is perfectly fine, which is why this Easy/Medium version differs from its Hard sibling.
k: Fixing the middle index j decouples the problem into an independent left-max and right-max query.
Strict inequalities matter: equal prices cannot be chained even though indices increase.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force around each middle
a.i: For every j, scan i < j for the maximum profit with prices[i] < prices[j], and k > j for the maximum profit with prices[k] > prices[j]. O(n^2) is fine for n = 2000.
s: For each j from 1 to n-2, scan left and right as described.
If both sides found a candidate, update the answer.
Return -1 if no triplet was ever found.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n middles we scan both sides once

a.i: Precompute left[] with a Fenwick tree over compressed prices supporting prefix-max (query prices < p, then insert p), and right[] identically on the reversed array. Then combine in one pass. This scales to the Hard version.
s: Forward pass: left[j] = prefix-max query below prices[j], then insert profits[j].
Backward pass on the reversed arrays gives right[j].
Answer = max(left[j] + profits[j] + right[j]) over valid j.
a.t: O(n log n) — two Fenwick passes with binary-search compression
a.sp: O(n) — compression arrays and Fenwick trees

w: The brute force is the right interview answer here given n ≤ 2000; mention the Fenwick upgrade since the Hard version (n = 5e4) requires it. Pitfalls: using <= instead of < for price comparisons, and treating profit 0 as 'no candidate' (profits are ≥ 1 here, which makes the sentinel safe). Follow-up: solve the Hard variant directly.
